anaphora.name: Anaphora
anaphora.plain: Starting several clauses, sentences, or lines in a row with the same word or phrase. Each repeat adds pressure, and the changing endings carry the idea forward. Common in speeches because listeners feel the pattern without needing to see it.
anaphora.example: "We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields…" — Churchill
anaphora.confuse: Epistrophe repeats at clause *ends*; symploce does both at once.

epistrophe.name: Epistrophe
epistrophe.plain: Ending several clauses or sentences in a row with the same word or phrase. Where anaphora repeats the start, epistrophe repeats the finish, so each sentence lands on the same word with more force.
epistrophe.example: "…government of the people, by the people, for the people" — Lincoln
epistrophe.confuse: Anaphora repeats at beginnings; epanalepsis repeats a clause's opening word at its own end.

symploce.name: Symploce
symploce.plain: Anaphora and epistrophe at once: several clauses in a row share both their opening and their closing words, with only the middle changing. The fixed frame makes the changing part stand out.
symploce.example: "When there is talk of hatred, let us stand up and talk against it. When there is talk of violence, let us stand up and talk against it." — Bill Clinton
symploce.confuse: Not mere parallelism: symploce requires the identical words at both edges, not just matching grammar.

epanalepsis.name: Epanalepsis
epanalepsis.plain: Starting and ending a clause with the same word or phrase, so the sentence circles back to where it began. The loop suggests obsession, inevitability, or a self-contained truth.
epanalepsis.example: "The king is dead, long live the king."
epanalepsis.confuse: Anadiplosis repeats across a clause boundary (end of one, start of the next); epanalepsis circles within one unit.

anadiplosis.name: Anadiplosis
anadiplosis.plain: The last word of one clause becomes the first word of the next, linking them like a chain. The sequence feels like one thing leading to another. Stacked with rising importance, it becomes gradatio (climax).
anadiplosis.example: "Fear leads to anger. Anger leads to hate. Hate leads to suffering." — Yoda
anadiplosis.confuse: Gradatio is anadiplosis sustained up a ladder of intensity; epanalepsis circles back within a single clause.

gradatio.name: Gradatio / Climax
gradatio.plain: A chain of linked clauses, each picking up the last one's key word and raising the stakes until the sequence peaks. The step-by-step climb makes the final term feel earned.
gradatio.example: "…tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope." — Romans 5:3–4
gradatio.confuse: One chained repetition is anadiplosis; gradatio is the whole ascending staircase.

antithesis.name: Antithesis
antithesis.plain: Contrasting ideas placed in balanced, matching grammar, so the contrast shows in the sentence's shape. The symmetry suggests the two options are the only ones — which is why it sounds authoritative even when the split is false.
antithesis.example: "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times…" — Dickens
antithesis.confuse: Oxymoron compresses contradiction into a two-word phrase; antithesis holds the contrast across balanced clauses. Paradox asserts a contradiction as true rather than balancing alternatives.

asyndeton.name: Asyndeton
asyndeton.plain: Leaving out the connecting words a list would normally have: 'I came, I saw, I conquered' with no 'and.' The missing connectives speed things up and suggest the list could keep going.
asyndeton.example: "…and that government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish." — Lincoln (phrases without 'and')
asyndeton.confuse: Polysyndeton is its mirror — conjunctions multiplied rather than deleted. Brachylogia is asyndeton between single words.

polysyndeton.name: Polysyndeton
polysyndeton.plain: Using more connecting words than needed — and… and… and. Every item gets equal weight, and the series feels relentless. The effect can be biblical, breathless, or exhausted, depending on what is stacked.
polysyndeton.example: "And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat upon that house…" — Matthew 7:25
polysyndeton.confuse: Asyndeton deletes the connectives instead. Parataxis is the broader habit of coordination over subordination; polysyndeton is its most audible form.

parataxis.name: Parataxis
parataxis.plain: Clauses set side by side with no subordinating words — no because, although, or which. Everything sits on one level, so the reader supplies the connections the grammar leaves out. Typical of Hemingway and the King James Bible.
parataxis.example: "The sun rose. He walked to the window. The street was empty."
parataxis.confuse: Hypotaxis is its opposite: clauses nested by subordination. Asyndeton concerns missing conjunctions; parataxis concerns missing *hierarchy*.

isocolon.name: Isocolon
isocolon.plain: Phrases or clauses in a row with the same shape and nearly the same length. The equal weights make the sentence sound measured and deliberate: two parts suggest fairness, three suggest completeness.
isocolon.confuse: All isocolon is parallelism, but parallelism only requires matching structure, not matching *length and rhythm*.

parallelism.name: Parallelism
parallelism.plain: Putting matching ideas in matching grammatical form — phrases with phrases, clauses with clauses. The repeated structure says the items belong to one set and invites comparison. Break the pattern and the odd item stands out.
parallelism.example: "…conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition…" — Lincoln
parallelism.confuse: Isocolon adds equal length and rhythm; antithesis is parallelism put in service of contrast.

chiasmus.name: Chiasmus
chiasmus.plain: A two-part structure where the second half reverses the order of the first: A-B, then B-A. The crossing shape makes the sentence feel complete and closed. With the exact same words reversed, it is antimetabole.
chiasmus.example: "Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country." — JFK
chiasmus.confuse: Antimetabole reverses the *same words*; chiasmus may invert grammar or concepts without exact lexical repetition.

antimetabole.name: Antimetabole
antimetabole.plain: Repeating the same words in reverse order: A-B, then B-A. The mirror shape suggests the speaker has examined the idea from both directions. The most quotable form of chiasmus.
antimetabole.example: "When the going gets tough, the tough get going."
antimetabole.confuse: Every antimetabole is a chiasmus, but chiasmus can invert structure or sense without repeating the exact words.

polyptoton.name: Polyptoton
polyptoton.plain: Repeating a word in different forms — please/pleasure, judge/judgment. The root returns while its job changes, so the idea seems to run through the whole sentence.
polyptoton.example: "The Greeks are strong, and skilful to their strength, / Fierce to their skill, and to their fierceness valiant." — Shakespeare
polyptoton.confuse: Simple repetition (epizeuxis, diacope) repeats the same form; polyptoton morphs the word as it returns.

epizeuxis.name: Epizeuxis
epizeuxis.plain: Repeating a word immediately, with nothing in between: 'words, words, words.' The bare repetition reads as feeling too strong for grammar — grief, rage, or emphasis. The bluntest repetition device.
epizeuxis.confuse: Diacope repeats with a word or two intervening ("O villain, villain, smiling, damnèd villain"); epizeuxis allows no gap.

diacope.name: Diacope
diacope.plain: Repeating a word or phrase with a short interruption in between — 'Bond. James Bond.' The return of the word feels like insistence: once was not enough.
diacope.example: "Put out the light, and then put out the light." — Othello
diacope.confuse: Epizeuxis repeats with no gap at all; anaphora repeats only at clause openings.

conduplicatio.name: Conduplicatio
conduplicatio.plain: Taking a key word from one sentence and placing it prominently in the next. Unlike a pronoun, the full repetition insists on the word itself and carries the idea forward for another look.
conduplicatio.example: "This afternoon, this Easter afternoon, I saw a friend die. A friend I had known…"
conduplicatio.confuse: Anadiplosis requires the repeat at the exact seam (last word → first word); conduplicatio just needs the key word to recur early in the next unit.

metaphor.name: Metaphor
metaphor.plain: Saying one thing is another, without announcing the comparison. Because nothing flags the figure, the reader makes the connection themselves — which is why metaphor persuades where argument can't.
metaphor.example: "Juliet is the sun." — Romeo and Juliet
metaphor.confuse: Simile flags the comparison with like/as, keeping the two things separate. A metaphor sustained across a passage becomes extended metaphor or allegory; a strained, category-breaking one is catachresis.

simile.name: Simile
simile.plain: A comparison marked with like or as. The marker keeps both things visible, so the reader can test the resemblance. Similes can be more extreme than metaphors because the grammar admits they are comparisons.
simile.example: "My love is like a red, red rose." — Burns
simile.confuse: Drop the 'like' and it becomes metaphor. An epic simile extends the comparison over many lines with its own internal scene.

catachresis.name: Catachresis
catachresis.plain: A deliberately strained or 'wrong' metaphor — a word forced outside its normal use until the misfit itself is the effect. It reads as slightly broken on purpose, and makes an ordinary thing look new.
catachresis.example: "the watery part of the world" — Melville, for the ocean
catachresis.confuse: A dead metaphor ('table leg') no longer registers as figurative; catachresis keeps its torque — it must still feel misapplied.

metonymy.name: Metonymy
metonymy.plain: Replacing a thing's name with something associated with it — the crown for the monarchy, the White House for the administration. It works by association rather than resemblance, and the chosen stand-in shows what the writer takes to be essential.
metonymy.example: "The pen is mightier than the sword."
metonymy.confuse: Metaphor maps by resemblance; metonymy by association. Synecdoche is the special case where the substitute is a *part* of the whole.

synecdoche.name: Synecdoche
synecdoche.plain: A part standing for the whole (hired hands for workers) or the whole for a part (the law for one officer). The chosen part quietly makes an argument: calling sailors 'hands' reduces them to their labor.
synecdoche.confuse: A subtype of metonymy: synecdoche requires the part/whole relation specifically, not just any association.

personification.name: Personification
personification.plain: Giving human qualities, actions, or feelings to non-human things — nations conceive, winds sigh. Once a thing can act and want, it becomes a character in the sentence.
personification.example: "Because I could not stop for Death – / He kindly stopped for me –" — Dickinson
personification.confuse: Prosopopoeia goes further and gives the thing a speaking voice. Pathetic fallacy is personification of nature specifically, colored by the observer's emotion.

prosopopoeia.name: Prosopopoeia
prosopopoeia.plain: Giving an absent, dead, or non-human speaker actual lines to say — a voice, not just human qualities. The borrowed voice carries authority the author could not claim directly.
prosopopoeia.example: Cicero making the state of Rome herself rebuke Catiline.
prosopopoeia.confuse: Personification stops at attributing human qualities; prosopopoeia hands over the microphone.

pathetic-fallacy.name: Pathetic Fallacy
pathetic-fallacy.plain: Nature mirroring human emotion — storms for turmoil, spring for hope — as if the world felt what the character feels. Writers use it to let the setting carry the psychology.
pathetic-fallacy.example: The storm on the heath matching Lear's madness.
pathetic-fallacy.confuse: Ordinary personification needn't reflect anyone's inner state; pathetic fallacy specifically syncs outer weather to inner weather.

hyperbole.name: Hyperbole
hyperbole.plain: Exaggeration past literal belief, trusting the reader to scale it back. The point is not to deceive but to show intensity: the size of the overstatement measures the size of the feeling.
hyperbole.example: "I had to wait in the station for ten days — an eternity." — Conrad
hyperbole.confuse: Its opposite pole is understatement/litotes. When exaggeration collapses into the trivial for comic effect, that's bathos.

litotes.name: Litotes
litotes.plain: Stating something by denying its opposite — not bad, no small feat. The reader must flip the negative, and that extra step makes the understatement feel chosen. It signals modesty, irony, or control.
litotes.example: "having little or no money in my purse" — Melville
litotes.confuse: Meiosis is plain understatement without the negation mechanism; litotes specifically runs on negatives.

meiosis.name: Meiosis / Understatement
meiosis.plain: Deliberately calling something smaller than it is — a wound is 'a scratch.' The gap between the thing and its label makes the reader imagine the real size, which usually overshoots.
meiosis.confuse: Litotes is understatement achieved specifically through negation ('not unkind'); meiosis just shrinks the label.

irony.name: Irony
irony.plain: A gap between what is said and what is meant, between what a character knows and what the audience knows, or between expectation and outcome. Readers who catch the gap feel like insiders.
irony.example: "Brutus is an honourable man." — Antony, meaning the reverse
irony.confuse: Sarcasm is verbal irony weaponized at a target. Paradox asserts a real contradiction; irony merely means other than it says.

paradox.name: Paradox
paradox.plain: A statement that contradicts itself but turns out to be true in a way ordinary wording couldn't reach. It forces the reader to drop the frame in which the contradiction is impossible.
paradox.example: "The child is father of the man." — Wordsworth
paradox.confuse: Oxymoron is paradox compressed to a two-word collision ('living death'); antithesis balances opposites without asserting both are true.

oxymoron.name: Oxymoron
oxymoron.plain: Two contradictory words fused into one phrase — deafening silence, living death. The clash sits inside a single unit, so it can't be resolved by reading on; both terms must be held at once.
oxymoron.example: "Parting is such sweet sorrow." — Romeo and Juliet
oxymoron.confuse: Paradox is a contradictory *statement* that unfolds; oxymoron is the two-word spark.

allusion.name: Allusion
allusion.plain: An unmarked reference to another text, event, or figure, bringing its whole context along. Readers who catch it get a second layer of meaning, and the borrowed authority arrives without a citation.
allusion.example: "all men are created equal" inside the Gettysburg Address — importing the Declaration.
allusion.confuse: Quotation announces its borrowing; allusion smuggles it. Metalepsis is allusion at a further remove, referencing through a chain.

euphemism.name: Euphemism
euphemism.plain: A mild or indirect phrase in place of a harsh or taboo one — passed away, let go, collateral damage. Every euphemism is a small argument about what should not be looked at directly.
euphemism.example: "He is helping the police with their inquiries."
euphemism.confuse: Periphrasis is roundabout wording for any reason; euphemism specifically launders the unpleasant.

periphrasis.name: Periphrasis
periphrasis.plain: Saying something in more words than needed — a roundabout route instead of the direct name. The detour can elevate, evade, or characterize a speaker who can't say the plain thing.
periphrasis.example: "the finny tribe" for fish, in Augustan verse
periphrasis.confuse: Euphemism detours specifically around the offensive; pleonasm adds redundant words without rerouting the meaning.

pleonasm.name: Pleonasm
pleonasm.plain: Using more words than the grammar needs: 'I saw it with my own eyes.' Done deliberately, the surplus is emphasis or ritual fullness; done carelessly, it is padding.
pleonasm.example: "free gift", "burnt fire" — or ritual doubling in scripture
pleonasm.confuse: Tautology repeats the same *idea*; pleonasm repeats within one construction. Periphrasis reroutes; pleonasm just doubles.

zeugma.name: Zeugma
zeugma.plain: One verb governing two or more objects in different senses — often one literal, one figurative: 'She arrived in a taxi and a flood of tears.' The verb forks midway, and the fork reads as wit.
zeugma.example: "She arrived in a taxi and a flood of tears."
zeugma.confuse: Syllepsis is often used interchangeably; strictly, syllepsis requires the senses to differ while zeugma is any shared-verb yoking.

hendiadys.name: Hendiadys
hendiadys.plain: One complex idea expressed as two nouns joined by 'and' — sound and fury instead of furious sound. Splitting the idea makes both halves stand equal and gives the phrase a strange doubleness. A Shakespeare favorite.
hendiadys.confuse: Not a mere pair of things: in hendiadys the two nouns secretly name *one* thing.

hyperbaton.name: Hyperbaton
hyperbaton.plain: Breaking normal word order — object first, verb delayed, adjective after noun — so the displaced word lands with extra force. English word order is strict, so every violation is loud.
hyperbaton.example: "Some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall." — Measure for Measure
hyperbaton.confuse: Anastrophe is the mild, single-pair inversion; hyperbaton covers more violent or extended derangements.

anastrophe.name: Anastrophe
anastrophe.plain: Reversing the usual order of a word pair — adjective after noun, preposition after object: 'the forest primeval.' A small, controlled inversion that sounds older or more poetic.
anastrophe.confuse: The gentle end of hyperbaton's spectrum; periodic structure delays whole clauses, not word pairs.

periodic-sentence.name: Periodic Sentence
periodic-sentence.plain: A sentence that saves its main clause for the end, stacking qualifying material first. The reader carries everything forward until the close snaps it into meaning. Suspense built from grammar.
periodic-sentence.example: "Of Man's first disobedience, and the fruit / Of that forbidden tree… Sing, Heav'nly Muse." — Milton
periodic-sentence.confuse: The loose/cumulative sentence is its opposite: main clause first, modifiers trailing after.

cumulative-sentence.name: Cumulative (Loose) Sentence
cumulative-sentence.plain: Main clause first, then modifiers added after it, each one sharpening the picture. The grammar finishes early, so everything after reads as elaboration. The standard sentence of modern American prose.
cumulative-sentence.example: "He dipped his hands in the bichloride solution and shook them, a quick shake, fingers down, like the fingers of a pianist above the keys." — Sinclair Lewis
cumulative-sentence.confuse: The periodic sentence withholds its main clause until the end; cumulative delivers it first and then unspools.

parenthesis.name: Parenthesis
parenthesis.plain: An aside dropped into the middle of a sentence — set off by dashes, brackets, or commas — that interrupts without joining the grammar. It reads as a voice commenting on its own sentence as it goes.
parenthesis.confuse: An appositive renames the noun beside it; a parenthesis digresses without renaming anything.

apposition.name: Apposition / Appositive
apposition.plain: A noun phrase placed beside another to rename it: 'my brother, the doctor.' Each appositive is a second look at the same thing. Stacked, they redefine it step by step.
apposition.example: "124 was spiteful. Full of a baby's venom." — Morrison (appositive fragment)
apposition.confuse: Parenthesis interrupts without renaming; apposition always re-identifies the neighboring noun.

aposiopesis.name: Aposiopesis
aposiopesis.plain: Breaking off mid-sentence and leaving it unfinished — a dash into silence. What goes unsaid reads louder than words: threat, grief, or the unspeakable, left to the reader.
aposiopesis.example: "I will have such revenges on you both, / That all the world shall— I will do such things—" — King Lear
aposiopesis.confuse: Ellipsis omits words the reader can reconstruct; aposiopesis abandons the sentence at a cliff edge.

ellipsis.name: Ellipsis
ellipsis.plain: Leaving out words the grammar needs but the context supplies: 'I took the high road; she, the low.' The reader restores what's missing, and the gap itself draws attention.
ellipsis.example: "And he to England shall along with you." — Hamlet
ellipsis.confuse: Aposiopesis breaks off irrecoverably; elliptical omissions are recoverable from the surrounding grammar.

brachylogia.name: Brachylogia
brachylogia.plain: Extreme compression: single words strung together without connectives. Each word gets a full beat, and the missing grammar reads as urgency or command.
brachylogia.example: "We real cool. We / Left school." — Gwendolyn Brooks
brachylogia.confuse: Asyndeton omits conjunctions between phrases or clauses; brachylogia does it between bare words.

alliteration.name: Alliteration
alliteration.plain: Repeating the first consonant sound across nearby words. The shared sound binds the words together before their meanings do. The oldest structuring device in English verse, and the fastest way to make a phrase stick.
alliteration.example: "would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world" — Melville's w's
alliteration.confuse: Assonance repeats vowel sounds; consonance repeats consonants anywhere in the word, not just initially.

enjambment.name: Enjambment
enjambment.plain: A verse line that ends before its sentence does, pushing the reader across the break. For a moment the line means one thing alone and another once continued, and the carried-over word lands with momentum.
enjambment.example: "April is the cruellest month, breeding / Lilacs out of the dead land…" — Eliot
enjambment.confuse: An end-stopped line completes its grammar at the break. Caesura is a pause *inside* the line, not at its edge.

in-medias-res.name: In Medias Res
in-medias-res.pron: in MAY-dee-ahs RACE / ɪn ˈmɛdiəs ˈreɪs
in-medias-res.plain: Starting in the middle of the action, with backstory held for later. The reader arrives in a world already moving and must catch up by inference — which creates instant momentum.
in-medias-res.example: Paradise Lost opening after the fall of the rebel angels, not before.
in-medias-res.confuse: Analepsis (flashback) is how the deferred backstory later arrives; in medias res is the choice of entry point itself.

prolepsis.name: Prolepsis
prolepsis.plain: Anticipation: treating a future event as already settled, or answering an objection before it is raised. In stories, the flash-forward; in argument, the pre-emptive answer.
prolepsis.example: "Many years later, as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendía was to remember…" — García Márquez
prolepsis.confuse: Analepsis looks backward (flashback); prolepsis looks forward. In rhetoric, procatalepsis is the objection-answering subtype.

analepsis.name: Analepsis
analepsis.plain: The flashback: the narration steps out of the present to tell earlier events. The past arrives when it will mean most, which shows that the narrator, not the calendar, controls the order.
analepsis.confuse: Prolepsis is its forward-facing mirror, the flash-forward.

apostrophe-device.name: Apostrophe
apostrophe-device.plain: Turning from the real audience to address someone absent, dead, or something non-human: 'O wild West Wind.' The turn dramatizes feeling too big for the room, and makes the reader an overhearer.
apostrophe-device.example: "O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?"
apostrophe-device.confuse: Direct address speaks to the present audience ('Reader, I married him' sits between the two); invocation is apostrophe petitioning for aid.

invocation.name: Invocation
invocation.plain: A formal appeal to a muse, god, or power to inspire the work — the classic epic opening. It performs humility and ambition at once, and signals which tradition the work claims.
invocation.confuse: Apostrophe is any address to the absent; invocation specifically petitions for aid at a threshold.

rhetorical-question.name: Rhetorical Question
rhetorical-question.plain: A question asked for effect, with the answer assumed rather than sought. The reader supplies the answer — and, having supplied it, half believes it.
rhetorical-question.example: "Hath not a Jew eyes?" — The Merchant of Venice
rhetorical-question.confuse: Hypophora asks and then *answers its own* question; aporia performs genuine (or staged) doubt.

apophasis.name: Apophasis
apophasis.plain: Claiming you won't mention something while mentioning it: 'I won't dwell on his record.' The denial performs innocence while the content lands anyway.
apophasis.example: "I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him."
apophasis.confuse: Paralipsis and praeteritio are near-synonyms; irony is the wider genus of saying-other-than-meaning.

aphorism.name: Aphorism
aphorism.plain: A short, freestanding statement of general truth, polished until it sounds inevitable. The balance and brevity make an opinion feel like a law.
aphorism.example: "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife." — Austen (ironic aphorism)
aphorism.confuse: A maxim instructs conduct; an epigram jokes; the aphorism claims truth. Austen's is an aphorism wearing irony.

epithet.name: Epithet
epithet.plain: A characterizing adjective or phrase attached to a name — wine-dark sea, swift-footed Achilles. Repeated, it fuses with the noun and becomes part of the identity.
epithet.confuse: A transferred epithet (hypallage) moves the adjective to the wrong noun: 'a sleepless night' — the night wasn't sleepless; you were.

hypallage.name: Transferred Epithet / Hypallage
hypallage.plain: An adjective moved from the noun it logically belongs to onto a neighbor — a sleepless night, a condemned cell. The feeling leaks from the person into the scenery, and the misplacement is the point.
hypallage.example: "Once more the storm is howling, and half hid / Under this cradle-hood and coverlid / My child sleeps on" → "murderous innocence of the sea" — Yeats
hypallage.confuse: A plain epithet sits on its rightful noun; hypallage is the deliberate misdelivery.

enumeratio.name: Enumeration / Accumulatio
enumeratio.plain: Piling up details, examples, or charges into a deliberate list. By the tenth item the reader stops weighing and starts accepting: the size of the pile becomes the argument.
enumeratio.example: Whitman's catalogues of trades and bodies in "Song of Myself"
enumeratio.confuse: Simple listing is neutral; enumeratio is a list with rhetorical intent — the pile *is* the point. Congeries is the near-synonym.

tmesis.name: Tmesis
tmesis.plain: Splitting a word or set phrase and wedging another word inside: abso-bloody-lutely. The interruption makes the emphasis feel involuntary, as if the feeling burst the word open.
tmesis.confuse: Infixation is the linguist's term for the same surgery; parenthesis interrupts a sentence, tmesis interrupts a single word.

bathos.name: Bathos
bathos.plain: A sudden drop from the lofty to the trivial. Accidental, it is failed grandeur; deliberate, it is comedy that punctures pretension by letting the reader feel the fall.
bathos.example: "Here thou, great Anna! whom three realms obey, / Dost sometimes counsel take — and sometimes tea." — Pope
bathos.confuse: Pathos moves; bathos drops. Anticlimax is the structural name for the same descent.

stichomythia.name: Stichomythia
stichomythia.plain: Dialogue traded in quick single lines, each speaker capping or reversing the other's words. The exchange works like fencing: every line answers the last.
stichomythia.confuse: Ordinary quick dialogue lacks the line-for-line symmetry and echoed vocabulary that make stichomythia a formal duel.

solecism.name: Solecism
solecism.plain: A deliberate breach of standard grammar — dialect, double negatives, non-standard forms — used for effect. In fiction it builds voice: the 'error' makes the speaker real.
solecism.example: "You don't know about me without you have read a book…" — Huck Finn
solecism.confuse: An accidental solecism is just an error; the device requires the wrongness to be chosen and characterizing. Enallage is the classical name for expressive grammatical substitution.

neologism.name: Neologism
neologism.plain: An invented word, coined outright or fused from existing parts. The reader works it out from its pieces and its context, and the small act of decoding makes the word theirs.
neologism.example: "'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves…" — Carroll
neologism.confuse: Catachresis misuses an existing word; neologism mints a new one. A portmanteau is a neologism made by fusion (slithy = slimy + lithe).

enthymeme.name: Enthymeme
enthymeme.plain: An argument with one premise left unstated, trusting the audience to supply it. What the audience supplies, it doesn't question — the missing premise is where the persuasion hides.
enthymeme.example: "He's a politician, so check your wallet." (Suppressed: all politicians are venal.)
enthymeme.confuse: A full syllogism states both premises; an enthymeme's power is exactly the one it doesn't state.

correctio.name: Correctio / Epanorthosis
correctio.plain: Saying something and immediately revising it: 'a hundred — no, a thousand times.' The visible self-correction performs sincerity while keeping both versions on the record.
correctio.example: "Sixty Million and more" — Morrison's epigraph revising itself upward
correctio.confuse: Aposiopesis abandons the sentence; correctio revises it in flight and keeps going.

metalepsis.name: Metalepsis
metalepsis.plain: A figure built on another figure — a reference the reader reaches only through a chain of associations. In narrative, it names a break between levels: a character addressing the author, a narrator entering the story.
metalepsis.example: "I have drunk milk from the cow that scattered the seed" — reaching an idea through chained figures
metalepsis.confuse: Simple metonymy makes one associative hop; metalepsis needs at least two. The narrative sense (frame-breaking) is the common modern usage.

free-indirect-discourse.name: Free Indirect Discourse
free-indirect-discourse.plain: Third-person narration that takes on a character's voice and judgments without quotation marks or 'she thought' tags. The character's mind arrives inside the narrator's sentences, and irony lives in the gap between the two.
free-indirect-discourse.example: "What a lark! What a plunge!" — Mrs. Dalloway's mind in the narrator's sentence
free-indirect-discourse.confuse: Direct discourse quotes; indirect discourse reports ('she thought that…'); FID deletes the tag and lets the voices blend.

stream-of-consciousness.name: Stream of Consciousness
stream-of-consciousness.plain: Prose imitating the raw flow of a mind — jumps of association, unfinished syntax, memory and sensation mixed together. The grammar loosens because the mind hasn't sorted itself into sentences yet.
stream-of-consciousness.example: Benjy's section of The Sound and the Fury.
stream-of-consciousness.confuse: Free indirect discourse keeps the narrator's grammatical order while borrowing the character's voice; stream of consciousness lets the order itself dissolve.

passive-voice.name: Passive Voice
passive-voice.plain: The subject receives the action instead of doing it: 'mistakes were made.' The construction can drop the actor entirely, and that omission is always information — modesty, evasion, or anonymity.
passive-voice.example: "…upon this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty" — agency diffused into the passive participles
passive-voice.confuse: Not every 'to be' + participle is passive ('he was tired' is adjectival); the test is whether an agent has been displaced.

cleft-sentence.name: Cleft Sentence
cleft-sentence.plain: Splitting a simple sentence in two to spotlight one part: 'It was Ishmael who survived' instead of 'Ishmael survived.' Grammar's way of stressing a word without italics.
cleft-sentence.example: "It was the best butter." → "It was a bright cold day in April…" — Orwell's it-frame
cleft-sentence.confuse: A pseudo-cleft uses 'what' ('What he wanted was peace'); both are focus machines, differing in which slot gets the spotlight.

juxtaposition.name: Juxtaposition
juxtaposition.plain: Two things placed side by side with no stated connection, letting the pairing make the meaning. The writer supplies the closeness; the reader supplies the relation.
juxtaposition.example: "The apparition of these faces in the crowd; / Petals on a wet, black bough." — Pound
juxtaposition.confuse: Antithesis states its contrast in balanced grammar; juxtaposition just sets the two things down and walks away.

foreshadowing.name: Foreshadowing
foreshadowing.plain: Details planted early that quietly predict later events, fully readable only in hindsight. On first pass they set the mood; on second pass they prove the design.
foreshadowing.example: Romeo's "my mind misgives / Some consequence yet hanging in the stars."
foreshadowing.confuse: Prolepsis states the future outright; foreshadowing only seeds it. Chekhov's gun is its craft maxim.

symbol.name: Symbol
symbol.plain: A concrete thing that carries meanings beyond itself, gathering more each time it returns. Unlike allegory's one-to-one code, a live symbol never runs out: the green light is longing, the future, money, America — and none of these exactly.
symbol.example: The green light at the end of Daisy's dock — Gatsby
symbol.confuse: Allegory fixes the correspondence; metaphor asserts it locally in one sentence. A symbol earns its meanings by recurrence.

archaism.name: Archaism
archaism.plain: Deliberately old-fashioned language — four score, thou — used for its aura. Old words bring their era's authority with them: scripture, epic, law.
archaism.example: "Four score and seven years ago…" — Lincoln
archaism.confuse: Allusion points to a specific prior text; archaism borrows a period's diction wholesale without citing anyone.

parrhesia.name: Parrhesia
parrhesia.plain: Bold, risky frankness — saying the dangerous thing plainly, often flagging the risk first: 'I'll speak freely.' The announced candor buys trust: a speaker willing to offend seems unwilling to lie.
parrhesia.example: Kent to Lear: "be Kent unmannerly, / When Lear is mad… What wouldst thou do, old man?"
parrhesia.confuse: Apophasis pretends *not* to say the thing; parrhesia says it and points at its own daring.

metabasis.name: Metabasis
metabasis.plain: A brief transition that sums up what has been said and previews what comes next: 'So much for the causes; now the consequences.' The argument showing the reader its map.
metabasis.example: "So much for the causes; now for the consequences."
metabasis.confuse: Metanoia revises a statement; metabasis merely pivots between sections.

amplificatio.name: Amplificatio
amplificatio.plain: Returning to the same point with more force each time — repeating, stacking, escalating until the idea fills the frame. Where a list adds instances, amplification adds size.
amplificatio.example: Cicero circling Catiline's treachery in wave after rising wave.
amplificatio.confuse: Enumeratio lists; amplificatio inflates. Auxesis is its close kin, arranging terms in ascending force.

aporia.name: Aporia
aporia.plain: Performed doubt: the speaker wonders aloud what to say, or whether it can be said at all. Sometimes the doubt is real, sometimes staged; either way it dramatizes honesty and difficulty.
aporia.example: "To be, or not to be, that is the question" — deliberation as spectacle
aporia.confuse: A rhetorical question presumes its answer; aporia performs not having one.

onomatopoeia.name: Onomatopoeia
onomatopoeia.plain: Words that sound like what they mean — buzz, crack, murmur. At full strength, whole lines can be built so their sound acts out the event they describe.
onomatopoeia.example: "The moan of doves in immemorial elms, / And murmuring of innumerable bees" — Tennyson
onomatopoeia.confuse: Alliteration and assonance pattern sounds without imitating anything; onomatopoeia requires the sound-sense match.

assonance.name: Assonance
assonance.plain: Repeating vowel sounds in nearby words — the deep green sea. Long vowels slow a line down; short ones speed it up. It binds lines together below conscious notice.
assonance.example: "in Xanadu did Kubla Khan / A stately pleasure-dome decree" — the a's and u's
assonance.confuse: Alliteration repeats initial consonants; consonance repeats consonants anywhere; assonance is vowels only.

mythopoesis.name: Mythopoesis
mythopoesis.plain: Writing pitched at the level of origin stories, where characters become archetypes and events explain the world, not just the plot. Genealogies, epithets, and ritual repetition are its tools.
mythopoesis.example: "Many years later… his father took him to discover ice." — García Márquez founding a world
mythopoesis.confuse: Allusion borrows an existing myth; mythopoesis manufactures the mythic register itself.

enargeia.name: Enargeia / Vivid Specificity
enargeia.plain: Description so concrete and sensory that the audience seems to see it rather than read it. The precision does persuasive work: specific detail vouches for the whole account.
enargeia.example: Homer lingering on the boar's-tusk helmet, strap by strap.
enargeia.confuse: Ekphrasis is enargeia aimed at an artwork; imagery is the broad modern term without the persuasive charge.
